title: 1 Samuel 19:18–24
context: David flees to Samuel at Ramah, and they stay at Naioth. Saul sends three groups of messengers to seize David, but each is overcome by God’s Spirit and prophesies; when Saul comes himself, he too prophesies and lies down before Samuel. The episode explains the saying “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (compare 10:11–12). Both traditions read it as shared ground: God protects David without violence, and Saul’s experience is a check on his pursuit rather than a sign of restoration.

verses.text: Now David fled and escaped, and came to Samuel at Ramah, and told him all that Saul had done to him. He and Samuel went and lived in Naioth.
verses.arminianNotes:
David flees to Samuel at Ramah and tells him everything Saul has done; they go to stay at Naioth. David seeks the prophet who anointed him.

Arminian readers see David turning to God’s appointed prophet in his distress.
verses.reformedNotes:
David returns to Samuel, who anointed him in 16:13. The location of Naioth within Ramah is uncertain; it may refer to a prophetic dwelling place.

Reformed readers see David finding refuge with God’s servant. Both traditions read this as shared ground about seeking godly counsel in danger.

verses.text: Saul was told, saying, “Behold, David is at Naioth in Ramah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul is told that David is at Naioth in Ramah. The pursuit continues.

Arminian readers see Saul persisting in his chosen course despite every check. Each new report draws him further into pursuit.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul’s informants keep him aware of David’s movements. The scene is set for a confrontation.

Reformed readers see the conflict moving toward God’s intervention. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that Samuel’s presence makes Naioth a place where God’s authority is especially evident.

verses.text: Saul sent messengers to seize David; and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, God’s Spirit came on Saul’s messengers, and they also prophesied.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul’s messengers see the prophets prophesying with Samuel at their head, and God’s Spirit comes on them, and they also prophesy. God halts the mission.

Arminian readers see God protecting David without violence. The messengers are overwhelmed, not harmed.
verses.reformedNotes:
God’s Spirit overrides Saul’s orders. The messengers cannot carry out their task.

Reformed readers likewise see God’s sovereign protection. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s power over human plans; the nature of the prophesying is not described in detail.

verses.text: When Saul was told, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul sends two more groups of messengers, and each prophesies. The pattern repeats three times.

Arminian readers see Saul refusing to read the warning signs. His persistence is self-defeating and only repeats the failure.
verses.reformedNotes:
The threefold repetition emphasizes God’s control. No messenger can seize David.

Reformed readers see God thwarting Saul’s intentions completely. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the narrative’s quiet humor as each attempt fails in the same way.

verses.text: Then he also went to Ramah, and came to the great well that is in Secu: and he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” One said, “Behold, they are at Naioth in Ramah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul goes to Ramah himself, reaching the great well at Secu, and asks where Samuel and David are. The location of Secu is uncertain.

Arminian readers see Saul determined to act personally where his servants failed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul takes matters into his own hands. He is told they are at Naioth.

Reformed readers see Saul approaching a confrontation with God’s power. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, with the stage now set for what happens when Saul himself arrives.

verses.text: He went there to Naioth in Ramah. Then God’s Spirit came on him also, and he went on, and prophesied, until he came to Naioth in Ramah.
verses.arminianNotes:
On the way to Naioth, God’s Spirit comes on Saul, and he prophesies as he goes. The king is overtaken like his messengers.

Arminian readers see God restraining Saul without removing his responsibility for his intentions.
verses.reformedNotes:
God’s Spirit comes on Saul as it came on his messengers. He cannot reach David.

Reformed readers see God’s power over even a hostile king. Both traditions commonly read this experience as a means of protecting David rather than a sign of Saul’s restoration to favor.

verses.text: He also stripped off his clothes. He also prophesied before Samuel and lay down naked all that day and all that night. Therefore they say, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul strips off his clothes, prophesies before Samuel, and lies down all day and night; people ask, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” The saying also appears in 10:11–12.

Arminian readers see Saul humbled before Samuel.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Hebrew may refer to removing outer garments; interpreters differ. The scene is one of humiliation rather than honor.

Reformed readers see God disarming Saul’s pursuit. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without inventing disagreement about the prophesying and noting the contrast with 10:11–12.
